name: kdb+
vendor: KX (KX Software Limited, majority owned by TA Associates)
license: Proprietary, licence key required (free KDB-X Community Edition within limits); the KDB-X Python wrapper is Apache 2.0 apart from its bundled `q.so`
summary: A columnar time-series database that is also an interpreter for q, an array language, used for market data across trading and risk.
intro: kdb+ is one small binary, about 800 KB, that is both a database and the interpreter for q, an array language descended from APL. A table is a set of columns held as arrays in memory, and q applies each operation to a whole column at once, so analytics run inside the database instead of in a separate stored-procedure language. On disk a table is splayed: a directory with one file per column, mapped into memory rather than loaded, so a query reads only the columns it names. Large tables are also partitioned, usually one splayed directory per day. The classic setup, kdb+tick, is a handful of q processes talking over q’s own IPC protocol: a tickerplant receives the feed, can log it to a file for recovery and publishes it to subscribers; a real-time database (RDB) keeps today’s rows in RAM; and a historical database (HDB) serves past days from disk. Built-in as-of joins (`aj`) match each trade with the quote in force at that moment.

KX now sells kdb+ as KDB-X, generally available since November 2025: the same engine, backward compatible, plus Python (KDB-X Python, formerly PyKX), SQL, a Parquet module, reads from object storage and a PostgreSQL wire-protocol proxy. Every copy needs a licence key from KX. The Community Edition is free for personal and commercial use with no expiry, within limits: 16 GB of RAM for q, one physical or virtual instance, 4 secondary threads and 16 connections per q process. Above that, KDB-X is priced by memory: on 2026-10-06 the list price was $1,822.92 a month for 32 GiB and $5,468.25 for 64 GiB, with quotes above 128 GiB. KX became majority owned by the private equity firm TA Associates in July 2025 and merged with OneTick, a market data and surveillance vendor, that September.
strengths: Fast scans, aggregations and time joins over columns of tick data: as-of joins, bucketing with `xbar` and nanosecond timestamps are part of the language
Data and logic live in one process, so calculations run where the data is instead of shipping rows to an application
A plain on-disk layout: each column is a file, each day a directory, and the only stored metadata besides names is a `.d` file listing column order
Three decades of production use in capital markets, where the tickerplant, RDB and HDB pattern is widely known
KDB-X Community is free for commercial use within its limits, and Python and SQL interfaces let people start without learning q
limits: Closed source and licence-keyed: every install needs a key from KX, and use beyond Community limits (16 GB RAM, one instance, 4 threads, 16 connections per process) is priced per GiB of memory, about $1,823 a month for 32 GiB at list price
q is a terse APL-family language that few developers know; Python and SQL interfaces help, but tuning and the tick processes are still written in q
Not a self-managing cluster: scaling out means designing and running your own set of tickerplants, RDBs, HDBs and gateways
The older free licence, kdb+ on demand Personal Edition, is non-commercial only, must reach KX’s servers about once a minute, times out after six months and forbids publishing benchmark results
The product line is in flux: new features now ship in KDB-X, and the company changed hands in 2025 and merged with OneTick

sections.title: The processes in a kdb+tick system
sections.intro: A typical deployment is several q processes, each with one job. They call functions on each other over q’s IPC protocol.

items.name: Feed handler
items.text: Converts an exchange or vendor feed into q messages. Usually written in C, C++, Java or C#.

items.name: Tickerplant
items.text: Receives the messages, can write them to a log file for recovery, and publishes them to subscribed processes, immediately or in small batches.

items.name: Real-time database (RDB)
items.text: Holds the current day’s data in memory for sub-millisecond queries. KX’s tick guide suggests RAM of at least four times the expected daily data.

items.name: Intraday database (IDB)
items.text: When memory runs short, recent data is written to disk in small time partitions so the RDB can stay lean.

items.name: Historical database (HDB)
items.text: Date-partitioned, splayed tables on disk, memory-mapped when queried. At end of day the day’s data is sorted by instrument and then time before it is written.

story: Arthur Whitney began building trading systems at Morgan Stanley in 1988, around a terabyte of market data and a pairs-trading desk, using his own version of APL. In 1993 he and Janet Lustgarten founded Kx Systems to sell K, a smaller successor language. He kept rewriting K every few years, and kept storing data by column, which he had done since the 1970s: when you want time, price and size for one stock on one day, you read just those columns.

In 2003 Kx released q and the kdb+ database together. q is K with about 50 table operations added and English keywords instead of symbols, so a database query looks a little like SQL. Banks adopted it for tick data, where a day of trades and quotes fits in memory and years of history sit on disk.

First Derivatives, a Northern Irish firm, took control of Kx in 2014 and agreed in 2018 to buy out the founders’ remaining shares. In July 2025 TA Associates acquired FD Technologies, and KX relaunched kdb+ as KDB-X with Python, SQL and a free commercial Community Edition.

choices.why: Market data queries touch a few fields across many rows. Whitney said that to get one stock’s activity for a day you need only four columns, so a column store needs four seeks and a few megabytes of reading.

choices.choice: Keep today in memory, history on disk
choices.why: Whitney’s rule was to set things up so “the hot stuff is in memory”. During the day data stays sorted by time; at end of day it is sorted by instrument and then time and written to disk sequentially.

choices.choice: Make the database and the language one thing
choices.why: kdb+ tables are q objects written to the file system and mapped back into memory, so there is no separate stored-procedure language to learn or to move data into.

choices.choice: English words instead of APL symbols
choices.why: q sits on the 2000 implementation of K but adds named table operations and SQL-like `select` expressions, which made it approachable for database work.
